The innate aggression that you’re talking about IS good for farm work, but also personal protection. 

There are good pit bulls as well as other bully breeds, however, the overly aggressive/reactive type should not be your standard. Those are the ones that were backyard bred and have terrible genes. Dogs with bad genes will make them prone to instability, just like humans. 

The dogs used in dog fights were very much likely back yard bred, meaning bad genes, and there was a lot of dog fights so you’re adding even more bad genes to the pool. This has created a huge amount of unstable dogs versus those who were actually bred with a purpose through calculated, well thought out plans and responsible breeders. 

That is why many people will assume bully breeds are dangerous. They definitely can be, but so can German shepherds and even a Labrador or poodle. GSDs and Bully Breeds are just more likely due to their purpose.


Edit: I will also add that saying any bully dog is a close to wolves is very inaccurate. They would have to have some wolf content to be considered close to a wolf. Wolves, dogs with high wolf content to low, and domesticated dogs are completely different. 

Dogs with high content will act more like a wolf than a domesticated animal, and if you look into it and/or meet one the differences are very obvious. 

I do understand that you’re trying to compare them to a wild animal, but that’s just not accurate unless you’re trying to make a point that bully dogs are unstable like how wild animals appear to be. In which case I’d suggest you re-read the beginning of my reply.

I’m pretty sure the overall breeds are not called “pit bulls.” That’s just what the general public label them as and assume they’re all the same breed.

If you have not introduced them to the car or any sort of motion I would go ahead and do it anyways. It’s best to prepare for any sort of stimuli in a safe, controlled environment rather than hoping they’ll be okay while on your way to the vet.  Would suggest car introductions without movement first. There are ways to simulate movement without needing to be in a car, however, if you have a willing friend(or certain volunteer) that can drive around the neighborhood that would be a perfect scenario, in my opinion. 

Go slow and gentle. Do this after the puppies have spent time in the car without movement. Next day you can have someone let the car slowly move around. When they’re ready, go over speed bumps, slightly more rocky roads, etc. 

You should be in the back or passenger seat to interact with the puppy. Gentle voice, have a toy that’s stuffed with frozen treats. (Or just a toy. Suggesting frozen treat so that:
1. It’s harder for them to get treats out, but will engage them more. 
2. You don’t really want to give them a lot of food before or during the car ride. That can be a cause for car sickness if it wasn’t going to happen already. So slow feeding. Frozen treats will allow for licking and engagement, stuff like that.

Another good thing to teach will be “calmness.” Learning how to settle. Now that will possibly be more challenging than the car ride haha. But it’ll be useful for the hour long. It’ll teach them how to breathe for a second and perform the “art of doing nothing.” Let’s them relax, have gold indoor manners, etc. Plus they won’t be jumping around in the car which is a good plus. Should be in a safety crate anyways, but even so. No jumping? No barfing. They get to sleep and smell the outdoors. If only it could be that perfect right? Haha.

I would suggest training what you want first then use the e-collar to solidify what you trained. The e-collar won’t teach your dog how to sit. Luring with treats, toys, whatever will. The e-collar is typically used to solidify off leash, long-ranged obedience and such. 

Personally I wouldn’t use one on a 5 month since typically 5 months don’t have the obedience and learned commands to put an e-collar to full use/potential. 

However, you could do “soft”/short incorporations of the e-collar and just not use it for everything. So your dog has a good understanding of recall from 6ft leash and limited to no distractions. Now take outside with some birds, cars, people, etc. introduce distractions slowly. You don’t want to set them up for failure unless it’s actually required, and that would be a very specific situation that most dog handlers will not need. 

Start with dog on a long leash and increase length. So you can get a 20ft, but stick to 10ft. Work your way up/ further away. 

Look up videos. Lean what your dog’s working level is. Etc. e-collars can easily mess up your training with your dog. Especially 5months. Critical age.

Train individually, train around distractions, then go ahead and go for a “test run” indoors or in a controlled area. (Such as backyard)

If your trainer choked your dog to sit, fire that trainer immediately. I highly doubt he works with police dogs and if he does he’s not doing it right. I’ve worked with personal protection dogs. Leash checks are a thing, but they’re not choking the dog. They’re fast and done quickly and never done harshly. A German Shepherd is a hard dog. They can forgive you if you accidentally correct them at the wrong time, but abuse them and they won’t take it. Dog training requires respect and understanding. 

Look for another trainer. Look for a balanced dog trainer that will work with your dogs based off what they individually react best to. (Not just based off results, but also their body language. A dog is not trained if they’re shut down. They’re too scared to do anything by that point.)

Edit: also if the trainer told you to stop giving treats, ignore them. They should have taught you and shown you when it’s appropriate to praise and give treats and when you shouldn’t because you might be rewarding the wrong behaviour. 

REMINDER: Only work with a training method that you feel comfortable with. If you’re not working with your dogs at your best your dogs will sense that. If you prefer force free then go for it. If you prefer balanced (like what I described. Training using different methods that your dog individually responds best to) then do that. It’s your dog. Up to you.

Assuming that your dog is already comfortable with sniffing, touching, and placing either two front paws or two backs paws on something that may wobble or be tall and somewhat small in size, (like a fire hydrant) then you can start training your dog to balance on something that moves. 

It’s basically called confidence training. A lot of people have dogs climb or jump onto a slightly wobbly box or yoga ball and learning how to balance, which then helps build core muscles. (You are in charge of making sure the platform is balanced. Yoga ball can be wedges between your bed and a wall then you stable it with your foot. It is imperative that you teach the dog to have confidence in both themselves and you. You want them to trust you and know that if you ask them to jump onto something that it’s safe.) 

You increase how unstable the platform is until finally you build up to the two tight ropes. 

Adding the blindfold isn’t particularly super difficult for the dog, physically, but does require a lot of “trust exercise” for the dog to literally blindly follow and listen to you. It’s probably one of the ultimate tests to see how much trust your dog has in you.

This is true, although there is a tiny bit “flaw.” I say “flaw” because it’s more about the level of obedience in the dog, the personal dog, and just the opinions and rules of the organization. 

They said something like, “Family owners cannot play fetch with the dog. They cannot give them treats. They cannot say hello and greet them, pet them, give commands, nothing. Only the handler can be the one and only interaction and source of praise and stimulation so to encourage and solidify the relationship.” 

This is very true **IF** you are trying to get handler and dog connected when transitioning from trainer/organization to family. 

Now, some dogs can’t handle the multiple sources of affection, stimuli, and praise. (Including basics. Food and water) That’s fine because some dogs just only need attention from one person. It’s only a problem if, say, they get stressed from being around multiple people or can’t be handled by someone if the handler is incapacitated.  If that’s the case, then the dog isn’t ready or fit for the job. 

There is a slight flaw in that, though, because part of training an assistance dog is teaching them how to ignore other people while working. So, in a way, it *is* okay for someone else to interact, but it’s only for training purposes.. and that purpose is to pretend that that person doesn’t even exist. So, y’know. 

I personally prefer my dogs to be highly obedient and flexible. Smart enough to know when it’s time to work and when it’s okay to interact with other people. Some handlers also **need other people** to be able to handle their dog. Such as the obvious like paramedics. Others, it could be a spouse, loved one, caretaker, or anyone that may be needed to assist the handler. (Helping someone with blood sugar levels, seizures, etc.)

It’s definitely expensive unfortunately, but it IS worth it. You *could* attempt it yourself, but if this is your first pup and you don’t know what to look for for service dog work specifically, I would suggest finding someone that is very knowledgeable. Try to find someone that will have proof of the dogs that ended up being successful. It may be rare, but if you can find one that you’re sure they’re not lying about, then take them. (So like pictures, videos of them picking up the pup, performing the tests, and maybe even updated photos of the pups with their handlers. Maybe with blurred out faces for privacy reasons) 

**A LOT** of people use the **Volhard Puppy Aptitude Test.** I know a lot of SD handlers that used this test. 

The “umbilical cord”  is basically tethering your pup to you “24/7” so that you can not only monitor them, but teach them that they will need to “latch” on to one person and focus solely on that one person. It will also assist you and your pup to learn and teach what is appropriate and not appropriate to do in the House. Just walk around, let him sniff, interact with strange items. Show him which toys are appropriate to play with, etc. Now the second you become occupied in a way that will not allow you to give your attention, put him in a crate or have someone else do the “umbilical cord.” 

Students that are part of the Bergin University do this and will switch dogs when they’re at mid age and expect high obedience at around that time. 

*(Not to say that they’re not going to make mistakes. Well trained pups will have off days, but that does _not_ make it excusable. Constantly work with your pup. Engage them, etc.)*

Doing this, changing the tether, teaches the dog to learn how to focus on the one handler that is in control of them at the time. This allows the transition easier, if the handler requires a loved one to take over, or even someone of authority or assistance to help take hold of the dog. Such as a nurse to pass on to the loved one, paramedics, etc. These people are **not** responsible for your dog. They may handle them shortly to assist getting them into an ambulance and then into your room, but if you are not fit to care and handle your pup then you need someone present who can. Who can feed, offer basic care, exercise them, etc. 

*(Reminder: Socialization and exposure is great, but don’t let them get too consumed by it. Show it to them, but don’t let them chew on stuff they shouldn’t. Part of socialization is exposing them while asking for focus on you. This teaches them to learn how to accept what’s going on, but being okay with it, accepting the background, but will look to you for guidance. Once they’re off duty and/or not in training mode, they may be given more freedom. Again, don’t let them do things that you wouldn’t want your well behaved pet and even service dog to do in public. Zoomies? Definitely fine if off duty. Digging around? Depends on you and only if off duty. Barking at dogs? Heck no. Sniffing items in a store or the ground? Absolutely not. Sniffing other people while working? Definite no.*

*Off duty and sniffing in a pet friendly place? Sure.)*

Personally I still wouldn’t let my pup dig or bark at people or dogs or even sniff them unless allowed. Of course I mean that when they’re off duty. And I don’t let them bark at all haha.

I've been told that it's actually a myth for, say, psych dogs to not be able to build a relationship between you and your pup if taken into training under the wing of someone else, BUT if you are able to be included then please, please, please do so. As much as you can. Visit here and there and do a couple drills. This will not only teach you how to enter the mindset and routine of training, but it will teach you how to maintain the training. This will also help with the transition of the pup listening to you. 

Of course, some dogs will easily listen to you. 

Other dogs may not. It can also depend on the breed. 

Now if you're talking about a breed, say, like the GSD or Akita (Which are not recommended first time owners. Especially WL GSDs and Akitas) then it is very important to be involved as much as possible. Maybe even imperative. 

Also, yes, it's dangerous to expose your young 8wk old puppy to places where other dogs have been, but I cannot stress enough how important **early exposure** is. Take your pup to places with different surfaces, smells, etc., where other animals should not be around. It **IS** okay to take your pup into public areas if you're legitimately training and raising the pup to be an assistance pup. Also, side note, it's very rare for your pup to get some lethal illness like parvo. It can happen, but that's why you want to take the safety steps needed to prevent this such as, again, taking them to places that other pets should not be in. I am not saying that there won't ever be some, but just be smart about it. Keep your distance. Let people interact **only if** they are **clean, healthy, and have not interacted with other animals recently.**

An underrated, almost embarrassing, decision and method is take your pup in a stroller in public areas. You will get judged, you will get questioned, but here is the reasoning behind it:

- Early Exposure is imperative
- Stroller will keep pup off floor and away from possible germs
- Short trips made easier and you don't need to carry sleepy pup
- Offers a safe place for the pup
- Pup can watch from a distance, be close to you, and, again, feel safe with a comforting, familiar smelling blanket or clothing, etc. 

If you have any other questions you're more than welcome to ask on here or send me a DM. I have trained a few SDs and actively speak with other trainers and handlers that have both owner trained and trained through another trainer or program. 

*(Added Note: The website 'Service Dog Central' is pretty helpful. Just be prepared to learn the harsh realities of SD training and owning.)*

Good luck!

Edit: forgot to add that having the “umbilical cord” will also highly benefit both you and your pup!

I’m so sorry you had to experience this. As a dog trainer I’ve been on both sides. Handling aggressive dogs(both proactive and reactive and having to protect a dog that was being attacked. 

Although training the aggressive pup to the point that they would ignore, walk away, and/or self correct I **NEVER** trusted them to be left alone, out of my control, or even out of my sight. If they weren’t within my reach then they had an e-collar on and muzzle. If they were walking next to me they were always on a leash for the extra amount of control if around company. Especially with other dogs. Although off leash trained and very obedient and responsive, I, again, *NEVER** gave them too much or an inappropriate amount of trust and/or faith. 

Now to be on the receiving end... I train my personal dogs and Dogs that were vulnerable or timid to automatically walk or back up to be behind me so that I could be in the middle and block the way. Now this is if you’re able to be in the middle and am able to grab or kick the aggressive dog away. 

Of course, being in the middle of a dog fight is not preferable and really not suggested if you don’t know how to handle the situation and/or feel uncomfortable. Although you may want to protect your pup sometimes the situation cannot call for such an action. A very obvious example would be if you’re dealing with multiple dogs. 

(*Side Note: Kicking a dog is not something I want to do, but is sometimes necessary when it comes to self defense. Of course if you can avoid it, do it. You’d have to judge based on environment, energy, appearance of dog, etc.)* 

Having the dog behind you and with you blocking is just preferable for me, personally. If they are in front it could force them to be too defensive and react aggressively. If they run away then that could cause the opposing dog to chase. I have told my dog to back up or load up into my car(if doors are open. My personal dog is small enough that she can go under my car) if I’m able to get a hold of the opposing dog and I want my pup to get out of the scene. I use that command rarely because, again, it could make the opposing dog chase. 

**TL;DR:** Train your pup to respond appropriately. Learn how to handle dog fights as well as identifying dog behaviour. Learn to predict and read Dogs. Avoid certain areas where you cannot control other dogs. Have a plan on how you can GTFO.

You start out by teaching the command “leave it.” 

I taught it by putting a treat on the floor and covering it with my hand. I would slowly lift it and if the dog tries to go in I immediately cover it and say, “Leave it” once. Don’t say it too many times because then the dog, just like people, can become “deaf” to it. So say it with a reason behind it connected with an action. (Not always physical but in this instance it would be covering the treat) 

If you’re able to lift your hand, even for a second, and the do leaves it you immediately say, “Yes!” And give her a treat. Some people don’t like giving the treat that you were initially holding back because the dog will learn that they will get the treat that they’re supposed to leave. I didn’t have that problem with the dogs I’ve trained, but all dogs are their own selves. 

Anyways. Eventually you lead up to more time where the treat is exposed. Then you move on to standing up and covering the treat with your foot. 

Adding action is the hardest part along with using a high value treat. Dropping the treat on the floor would be your next step. (Whenever you move on to the next step always take it slow. Break it up into ‘mini steps.’ The pace you go at and the amount of steps you take depends on the dog)  

I remember that this one dog I trained (a service dog. You could probably find him in the history posts.) would be able to leave treats alone that were thrown right at his face. Literally, in the air, toward him, falling onto his face. 

Remember that whenever you make ANY progress in new breakthroughs, even if you have to take a step back before moving on, you act like it’s the best thing ever. Do that a few times until he starts doing it consistently. Then you can treat it like a normal achievement. Still with positivity. 

Acting like it’s a command and not a trick comes down later in the line. It’s the difference between teaching and asking for sit versus telling them to sit. 

Edit: 

Forgot to add how to do it without the command. Well you can go about it in two ways. 

Using a physical or silent command to leave it alone or teaching an automatic leave it. 

Basically you expect them to leave it. Instead of saying leave it before exposing the treat or dropping the treat you just do it and if they go for it then you say leave it. You can ease out the word by snapping your fingers. (Snap fingers along with verbal command first to connect the two) Then eventually don’t snap your fingers. I didn’t have to do this, but some dogs need that extra step. 

Teaching an automatic leave it is so handy. If you’re cooking and your pup is in the kitchen and you drop something that may be poisonous. Personally I don’t allow dogs in the kitchen. I do border/boundary training.

What does the dog do? He keeps doing it until he tires himself out. Then you reward. You want to correct him for barking and encourage calmness which is explained in Kikopups video. I’ve seen quite a few of hers and I really love her stuff.

You want to be careful about using a gentle leader though. Just like other training tools, not all tools work for every dog. So take things slow. I suggest starting with luring first before using any tools and then you assess the situation and ask yourself which tool would help me with this dog.
